questions.stem: A scatter graph shows that as temperature increases, ice cream sales increase. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: When both variables increase together, this is a positive correlation. The points slope upwards from left to right.

questions.stem: As the age of a car increases, its value tends to decrease. This relationship shows:
questions.explanation: When one variable increases while the other decreases, this is negative correlation.

options.text: One variable causes the other to change
There is a pattern or relationship between the variables
The variables have the same units

questions.explanation: Correlation means there is a pattern or relationship. It does NOT mean one variable causes the other to change -- correlation is not causation.

questions.stem: A point on a scatter graph that lies far from the general trend is called:
questions.explanation: A data point that does not fit the general pattern or lies far from the other points is called an outlier.

questions.stem: If the points on a scatter graph are scattered randomly with no pattern, this shows:
questions.explanation: If points are scattered randomly with no discernible pattern, there is no correlation between the two variables.

questions.stem: Which type of data is displayed on a scatter graph?

options.text: Two numerical variables measured for the same items

questions.explanation: Scatter graphs plot pairs of numerical values, where each point represents two measurements taken from the same item or person.

questions.stem: A study finds strong positive correlation between shoe size and reading ability in children. The most likely explanation is:

options.text: A third variable (age) affects both -- older children have bigger feet and better reading ability

questions.explanation: This is a classic example where a third variable (age) causes both to increase. Correlation does not imply causation.
